lessons.title: Supersaturation and Nucleation
lessons.body:
Supersaturation is the driving force for sugar crystallization. It measures how much sugar is dissolved beyond the equilibrium saturation point at a given temperature. In practice, you create supersaturation by evaporating water or cooling a sugar solution. The supersaturation coefficient (S) is the ratio of sugar to water in the solution divided by the same ratio at saturation. For crystallization to occur, S must be above 1.0. But if S goes too high, you get unwanted spontaneous nucleation Ã¢Â€Â“ tiny crystals that ruin your product.

In African sugar factories, pan boilers control supersaturation by adjusting vacuum, steam pressure, and feed rates. A typical target for crystal growth is S between 1.2 and 1.4. At S below 1.1, crystals barely grow. Above 1.5, you risk nucleation and false grain. Use a refractometer or a microwave moisture analyzer to check dissolved solids (Brix) and temperature to calculate S. For example, at 70Ã‚Â°C, a saturated sucrose solution is about 76% solids. If your pan has 80% solids at 70Ã‚Â°C, S = (80/20) / (76/24) = 4.0/3.17 = 1.26 Ã¢Â€Â“ good for growth.

Nucleation is the birth of new crystals. You want controlled nucleation only when starting a strike. In batch pans, you introduce seed crystals (slurry of fine sugar in alcohol) at the right moment. Alternatively, you can nucleate by shocking the syrup Ã¢Â€Â“ dropping temperature or adding a small amount of powdered sugar. In continuous pans, nucleation happens naturally but must be balanced with growth to maintain crystal size.

Practical tip: Keep your pan clean. Scale and burnt sugar act as nucleation sites, causing fine grain. In many African factories, pan boiling is still manual Ã¢Â€Â“ watch the sight glass and feel the consistency. A drop of massecuite on a glass slide, viewed under a simple magnifier, shows crystal size. If you see many tiny crystals, reduce supersaturation by adding water or syrup. If crystals are few and large, increase evaporation. This hands-on skill is learned on the job.

Remember, supersaturation and nucleation are the heart of sugar boiling. Master them, and you control crystal size, yield, and molasses exhaustion. Poor control means lost sugar in molasses and poor quality.

lessons.title: Crystallization Methods: Batch and Continuous
lessons.body:
Sugar crystallization is done in vacuum pans. There are two main methods: batch and continuous. Batch pans are the traditional choice in many African sugar mills. They work in cycles: fill, concentrate, seed, grow, and discharge. A batch pan might take 2Ã¢Â€Â“4 hours per strike. You start by pulling a vacuum (around 600Ã¢Â€Â“650 mmHg) and feeding clarified syrup. As water evaporates, supersaturation rises. When you reach S=1.2Ã¢Â€Â“1.3, you add seed crystals or nucleate. Then you feed more syrup to grow crystals while maintaining supersaturation. Finally, you drop the massecuite (mixture of crystals and mother liquor) to a receiver.

Continuous pans are becoming more common, especially in larger factories. They have multiple compartments. Massecuite flows from one end to the other, with syrup feed and steam heating in each section. Continuous pans run 24/7, producing a steady stream of massecuite. They are more energy-efficient and easier to automate, but they require careful control to avoid fine grain. In Africa, continuous pans are found in countries like South Africa, Egypt, and Mauritius. Smaller mills often stick to batch because they are simpler and cheaper to maintain.

Which method to choose? Batch pans are flexible Ã¢Â€Â“ you can adjust for different sugar qualities (white, raw, soft). They are ideal for small-scale operations. Continuous pans need a steady supply of syrup and skilled operators. They give consistent crystal size but are less forgiving of fluctuations.

Key parameters for both: vacuum, temperature (around 65Ã¢Â€Â“75Ã‚Â°C), and supersaturation. You also need to control the rate of syrup addition. Too fast, and you create new crystals (nucleation). Too slow, and crystals stop growing. In batch pans, you use a "footing" Ã¢Â€Â“ a starting volume of syrup Ã¢Â€Â“ then build on it. In continuous pans, you maintain a constant level and density.

For a learner in a rural African setting, start with batch pans. Learn to read the massecuite: it should feel like thick honey. A simple test: take a sample, cool it, and rub between fingers Ã¢Â€Â“ you should feel grains, not a smooth paste. If smooth, you have too much fine grain. Adjust by adding more seed or slowing feed. With practice, you can produce good crystals without expensive instruments.

lessons.title: Centrifugal Separation of Crystals and Molasses
lessons.body:
After crystallization, you have massecuite Ã¢Â€Â“ a mix of sugar crystals and molasses. To separate them, you use centrifugals. These are machines that spin at high speed, using centrifugal force to throw the heavy molasses through a screen while retaining sugar crystals. In African sugar factories, you'll find batch centrifugals (often called "machines") and continuous centrifugals.

Batch centrifugals are common in small to medium mills. They work in cycles: load, spin, wash, unload. A typical cycle takes 3Ã¢Â€Â“5 minutes. You load about 500Ã¢Â€Â“800 kg of massecuite into a basket lined with a fine screen (0.06Ã¢Â€Â“0.08 mm openings). The basket spins at 1000Ã¢Â€Â“1800 rpm. Molasses flies out through the screen, and crystals stay inside. After spinning for 1Ã¢Â€Â“2 minutes, you spray water or steam to wash the crystal surface, removing remaining molasses. Then you spin again to dry, and finally unload the sugar.

Continuous centrifugals are used for low-grade massecuite (final molasses). They have a conical basket and operate continuously. They are more efficient for high-volume, low-purity work. But for high-grade sugar (white or raw), batch centrifugals give better washing and lower color.

Key controls: spin speed, screen condition, and wash water. If the screen is torn, crystals escape with molasses Ã¢Â€Â“ lost sugar. If you use too much wash water, you dissolve crystals and increase molasses purity. A good rule: wash with 3Ã¢Â€Â“5% water by weight of massecuite. In many African factories, operators judge by sight: the sugar should look bright, not sticky. If it's sticky, increase spin time or wash.

Safety is critical. Centrifugals are heavy and fast. Never open the cover while spinning. Ensure the basket is balanced Ã¢Â€Â“ uneven loads cause vibration and can damage the machine. After unloading, check the screen for holes. Replace worn screens promptly.

For a small-scale processor, a manual batch centrifugal might be affordable. But even a simple basket centrifuge can work: line a drum with cloth, spin it with a motor, and you can separate small batches. The principle is the same. The goal is to get clean crystals and molasses that can be further processed or sold.

lessons.title: Affination and Washing of Raw Sugar
lessons.body:
Raw sugar from centrifugals still has a thin film of molasses on the crystal surface. This film contains impurities, color, and ash. To produce white sugar, you must remove it. Affination is the process of mixing raw sugar with a heavy syrup (affination syrup) to soften the molasses film, then centrifuging to wash it off. It's like a pre-wash before refining.

In African refineries, affination is done in a mingler Ã¢Â€Â“ a horizontal trough with paddles. Raw sugar and affination syrup (about 70Ã¢Â€Â“75 Brix) are mixed for 5Ã¢Â€Â“10 minutes. The syrup dissolves the molasses coating. The mixture, called magma, is then fed to centrifugals. There, it is spun and washed with water. The washed sugar (affined sugar) has lower color and purity, ready for melting and further processing. The separated syrup (affination syrup) is recycled or used for molasses production.

If you don't have a refinery, you can still improve raw sugar quality by simple washing. In a batch centrifugal, after spinning off the main molasses, spray water directly onto the crystal bed. Use about 5Ã¢Â€Â“10% water by weight of sugar. Spin again to remove the wash water. This reduces surface molasses and improves sugar quality. But be careful: too much water dissolves sugar, reducing yield. In small-scale operations, a simple technique is to wash raw sugar in a drum with a small amount of hot water (60Ã¢Â€Â“70Ã‚Â°C), stir, and then filter or centrifuge. The wash water becomes a sweet syrup that can be reused.

Why affinate? Because raw sugar with high molasses film causes problems in refining: it increases color, ash, and refining costs. Affination reduces these by 50Ã¢Â€Â“70%. For direct consumption raw sugar (like in some African markets), a light wash is enough.

Practical tips: Use clean water. If water is hard, soften it or use condensate. Control temperature Ã¢Â€Â“ too hot dissolves crystals, too cold doesn't remove molasses. Aim for 60Ã¢Â€Â“70Ã‚Â°C. Check the color of the wash water: it should go from dark to light. When it runs clear, stop washing. In many African factories, affination is a manual job Ã¢Â€Â“ workers judge by eye. With training, you can produce better sugar for local markets.

lessons.title: Molasses Recovery and Utilization
lessons.body:
Final molasses is the heavy, dark syrup left after all recoverable sugar has been crystallized. It typically contains 45Ã¢Â€Â“55% sucrose, 10Ã¢Â€Â“20% reducing sugars, and 5Ã¢Â€Â“10% ash. In African sugar factories, molasses is a valuable by-product. Recovering it efficiently means maximizing sugar extraction and finding profitable uses.

Recovery starts with exhausting the molasses Ã¢Â€Â“ getting as much sugar out as possible. This is done by boiling the molasses to a higher concentration (around 85Ã¢Â€Â“90 Brix) and crystallizing again. The resulting sugar (called final molasses sugar or C-sugar) is low purity and often sent back to the affination stage. The remaining molasses is then centrifuged off. In many factories, this is done in continuous centrifugals. The key is to control supersaturation and temperature. If you over-boil, you get viscous molasses that won't crystallize. If under-boil, you leave sugar in molasses.

Utilization of molasses in Africa is diverse. The most common uses:
1. Animal feed: Molasses is mixed with roughage (like maize stover or bagasse) to make nutritious feed for cattle. It provides energy and improves palatability. A typical mix: 10Ã¢Â€Â“20% molasses, 80Ã¢Â€Â“90% roughage.
2. Ethanol production: Many African countries (e.g., Kenya, South Africa, Malawi) ferment molasses to produce ethanol for fuel or beverages. A tonne of molasses yields about 250Ã¢Â€Â“300 liters of ethanol.
3. Food and beverage: In some cultures, molasses is used in baking (gingerbread, cookies) or as a sweetener. It's also used to make traditional alcoholic drinks like mowin in Nigeria or muratina in Kenya.
4. Fertilizer: Molasses can be composted or applied directly to soil as a carbon source for microbes. It's also used in bio-fertilizer production.
5. Other industrial uses: Citric acid, yeast, and vinegar production.

For small-scale processors, selling molasses to local farmers for animal feed is often the easiest. You can also use it to make silage. To store molasses, keep it in sealed drums or tanks away from moisture. It can last for months. If you want to add value, consider small-scale ethanol distillation Ã¢Â€Â“ but that requires licenses and safety measures.

Recovering more sugar from molasses reduces waste and increases profits. Even a 1% increase in molasses exhaustion can mean significant extra income for a factory. So pay attention to boiling and centrifugation Ã¢Â€Â“ every crystal counts.

lessons.title: Crystal Size Distribution and Quality Control
lessons.body:
Crystal size distribution (CSD) is the range of crystal sizes in a sugar sample. It affects centrifugation, washing, and final product quality. A good CSD means most crystals are within a narrow size range Ã¢Â€Â“ uniform crystals. Poor CSD means many fine and coarse crystals mixed. In African sugar factories, CSD is controlled by crystallization and centrifugation.

Why does CSD matter? Uniform crystals centrifuge better: molasses drains evenly, washing is efficient, and sugar dries faster. Non-uniform crystals cause problems: fines clog screens, coarse crystals trap molasses, and you get inconsistent color. Also, buyers prefer uniform crystals Ã¢Â€Â“ they look better and dissolve predictably.

How to measure CSD? In a lab, you use a set of sieves (e.g., 0.5 mm, 0.8 mm, 1.0 mm, 1.2 mm). You weigh 100 g of sugar, shake through sieves for 5Ã¢Â€Â“10 minutes, and weigh the fraction on each sieve. Plot the results. A good white sugar might have 80% between 0.6 and 1.0 mm. For raw sugar, larger crystals (1.0Ã¢Â€Â“1.5 mm) are common. In the field, you can use a simple magnifier and a ruler. Take a sample, spread on a glass, and measure 20 crystals. Calculate the average and range. If you see many tiny crystals (fines) or huge ones, adjust your pan boiling.

Quality control also includes moisture, color, and ash. Moisture should be below 0.05% for white sugar, 0.1Ã¢Â€Â“0.2% for raw. Color is measured in ICUMSA units Ã¢Â€Â“ white sugar under 45, raw up to 2000. Ash indicates mineral content. In small operations, you can check moisture by drying a sample in an oven at 105Ã‚Â°C for 3 hours. Color by comparing to a standard chart.

To improve CSD, control nucleation and growth. In batch pans, seed with a uniform slurry. Avoid temperature shocks. In centrifugals, use the right screen and spin speed. If you have many fines, reduce supersaturation or add more seed. If crystals are too large, increase nucleation slightly.

Record your data. Keep a log of pan boiling times, temperatures, and CSD results. Over time, you'll see patterns. In many African factories, simple record-keeping has improved sugar quality by 10Ã¢Â€Â“20%. Train your operators to spot problems early. Quality control is not just for labs Ã¢Â€Â“ it's for everyone on the floor.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sugar Processing Plant Operations, Troubleshooting and Quality Benchmarks

This practical reference lesson consolidates the operational knowledge covered in Module 8 and translates it into a working field guide for sugar processors across Africa. Whether you run a small jaggery unit in Uganda, a vacuum pan house in Kenya, or a raw sugar mill in Nigeria or Eswatini, the numbers, checks and troubleshooting logic below are designed to be used on the factory floor â not just in the classroom. The focus is on the crystallisation, centrifugal and molasses recovery stages, because these determine your final yield, your product grade and, ultimately, your margin per tonne of cane or beet processed.

Why This Stage Decides Your Profit

In most African sugar operations, the pan house and centrifugal station are where the largest value is created or lost. Cane and beet prices are largely set by the market, but recovery efficiency, crystal quality and molasses exhaustion are all under your control. A one-point improvement in overall recovery on a 1,000 tonne cane per day (TCD) mill can translate into several tonnes of extra sugar per day â a direct contribution to gross margin.

The lessons in this module â supersaturation and nucleation, batch and continuous crystallisation, centrifugal separation, affination and washing, molasses recovery, and crystal size distribution (CSD) â should be read as one integrated system. A mistake in the pan (too high supersaturation) shows up as false grain in the centrifugal, poor purging, higher molasses purity and lost sugar. A mistake in the centrifugal (wrong screen, poor wash) shows up as high colour and ash in your raw sugar, which reduces your price or forces extra refining cost.

Key Operating Benchmarks

The table below gives typical operating ranges for vacuum pan and centrifugal stations in African raw and white sugar mills. These are reference figures â always confirm against your own factory's historical data and your equipment supplier's manual.

Table 1: Typical vacuum pan and centrifugal operating benchmarks
Parameter Typical Range Notes / Risk if Out of Range
Supersaturation coefficient (pan) 1.15 â 1.25 (nucleation zone 1.2 â 1.4) Above 1.4 causes false grain and fine crystals; below 1.1 dissolves existing crystals.
Massecuite brix at strike 88 â 92 Â°Bx (A-strike), 92 â 96 Â°Bx (C-strike) Too low gives weak crystals and poor exhaustion; too high causes pan boiling difficulty and high viscosity.
Centrifugal screen slot width 0.06 â 0.10 mm (raw), 0.04 â 0.06 mm (white) Too wide loses crystals to molasses; too narrow blocks purging and slows cycle time.
Wash water application (raw sugar) 2 â 5 % on massecuite mass Excess wash dissolves crystals and raises molasses purity; too little leaves high colour and ash.
Molasses purity (final, C-molasses) 32 â 40 (apparent purity) High purity means poor exhaustion â recoverable sugar is being sold as molasses.
Crystal size (MA, mean aperture) 0.6 â 1.2 mm (raw), 0.4 â 0.8 mm (white) Small crystals increase centrifugal load and colour; large crystals reduce surface area for washing.
Coefficient of variation (CV) of CSD < 30 % (good), 30 â 35 % (acceptable) High CV means uneven crystals, poor purging and inconsistent product.

Sources: FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin on sugar processing; Peter Rein, Cane Sugar Engineering (Verlag Dr. Albert Bartens); ICUMSA methods for sugar analysis. Ranges are indicative and should be verified against local factory data.

Troubleshooting the Pan and Centrifugal Station

Most day-to-day problems in the pan house and centrifugal station fall into a small number of categories. The table below links common symptoms to likely causes and corrective actions. Use it as a first-line diagnostic before calling the process chemist.

Table 2: Troubleshooting guide â crystallisation and centrifugal station
Symptom Likely Cause Corrective Action
False grain / fine crystals in massecuite Supersaturation too high; sudden temperature drop; seeding rate too low Reduce evaporation rate, raise pan temperature slightly, adjust seeding and check syrup brix.
Poor purging in centrifugal (long cycle) High molasses viscosity; low temperature; screen partly blocked; crystal size too small Check massecuite temperature, clean or replace screens, review crystal size and CV.
High colour in raw sugar Insufficient wash water; high colour in syrup; carry-over from clarifier Increase controlled wash water, review clarification and syrup colour, check affination performance.
High ash / conductivity in sugar Inadequate wash; high ash in syrup; poor affination of raw sugar Optimise wash water, review affination syrup purity and wash stages.
High molasses purity (poor exhaustion) Low crystal yield; short boiling time; high massecuite brix; poor crystallisation management Review C-strike brix, boiling curve, cooling crystallisation and re-melting of low-grade sugar.
Sticky or caked sugar in storage High moisture; high residual molasses film; high temperature at packing Improve drying and cooling, control wash and affination, check storage humidity.

Sources: Peter Rein, Cane Sugar Engineering; FAO sugar processing guidance; ICUMSA recommended methods. Adapted for African mill conditions.

Safety and Food Quality Warning

â  SAFETY AND FOOD QUALITY WARNING

Sugar processing involves hot massecuite (typically 60â80 Â°C), high-speed centrifugals, caustic and acid cleaning chemicals, and steam under pressure. Never open a centrifugal basket while it is rotating, and never bypass interlocks. Hot massecuite and molasses cause severe burns â always wear heat-resistant gloves, face shields and aprons when sampling or purging. Cleaning chemicals (caustic soda, sulphamic acid, biocides) must be handled with appropriate PPE and never mixed. For food safety, raw sugar and molasses intended for human consumption must meet national and Codex microbiological and contaminant limits; molasses for animal feed must comply with feed safety standards. Refer to WHO/FAO Codex Alimentarius and your national bureau of standards for limits on heavy metals, pesticide residues and microbial contamination.

Africa Context: Small, Medium and Large Operations

Africa's sugar sector spans a wide range of scales. Small jaggery and open-pan units in Uganda, Tanzania, Malawi and Nigeria often operate without vacuum pans, relying on open boiling and manual stirring. Medium mills in Kenya, Zambia and Mozambique use batch vacuum pans and centrifugal stations. Large estates in Eswatini, South Africa, Sudan and Egypt operate continuous crystallisation and refinery-grade affination. The principles in this module apply across all scales, but the operating windows differ. For small units, the priority is consistent boiling, clean equipment and good hygiene. For medium and large mills, the priority shifts to recovery optimisation, energy efficiency and product quality consistency for both domestic and export markets.

Regional trade bodies such as the African Sugar Association and national sugar boards often publish annual production and quality data. Use these to benchmark your factory against peers. Where your molasses purity or CSD CV is worse than the regional average, investigate the pan and centrifugal station first.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Verify syrup brix and temperature before starting the strike; record in the pan log.
  • â Confirm supersaturation is within 1.15â1.25 before seeding; avoid false grain.
  • â Check centrifugal screens for damage or blockage at the start of every shift.
  • â Measure and record wash water flow â keep within 2â5 % of massecuite mass for raw sugar.
  • â Sample final molasses and record apparent purity; target below 40 for good exhaustion.
  • â Monitor crystal size (MA) and CV at least once per shift; target CV below 30 %.
  • â Confirm all PPE is worn during sampling, purging and chemical cleaning.
  • â Record all deviations and corrective actions in the shift handover log.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-scale sugar processing technologies (Agricultural Services Bulletin)
  • FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius â Food safety standards including sugars
  • ICUMSA â International Commission for Uniform Methods of Sugar Analysis
  • WHO â Guidelines on food safety and contaminants
  • African Sugar Association â Regional production and quality resources

Use this reference alongside the earlier lessons in Module 8. The numbers are starting points; your own factory data, calibrated instruments and trained operators are what turn them into consistent profit. In sugar processing, consistency is the product â and consistency comes from disciplined measurement, not guesswork.

quiz.q: What does supersaturation measure?
options: A) The amount of sugar dissolved beyond saturation
B) The temperature of the syrup
quiz.explanation: Supersaturation is the ratio of dissolved sugar to water compared to saturation, indicating excess sugar available for crystallization.

quiz.q: What is the target supersaturation coefficient for crystal growth?
quiz.explanation: At S between 1.2 and 1.4, crystals grow well without excessive nucleation.

quiz.q: What happens if supersaturation is too high?
quiz.explanation: High supersaturation causes unwanted nucleation, creating many fine crystals.

quiz.q: Which tool can be used to check dissolved solids for supersaturation?
quiz.explanation: A refractometer measures Brix (dissolved solids), which is used with temperature to calculate supersaturation.

quiz.q: What is nucleation?
options: D) Separation of crystals from molasses
quiz.explanation: Nucleation is the birth of new crystals, either spontaneously or by seeding.

quiz.q: In batch pans, how is nucleation typically controlled?
quiz.explanation: Seeding with fine sugar crystals provides controlled nucleation sites.

quiz.q: What is a common problem if a pan has scale or burnt sugar?
quiz.explanation: Scale and burnt sugar act as nucleation sites, causing fine grain.

quiz.q: Which crystallization method is more common in small African mills?
quiz.explanation: Batch pans are simpler, cheaper, and more flexible for small-scale operations.

quiz.q: What is the typical cycle time for a batch pan strike?
quiz.explanation: A batch pan strike usually takes 2 to 4 hours from fill to discharge.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of continuous pans?
quiz.explanation: Continuous pans are easier to automate and provide steady production.

quiz.q: What is massecuite?
options: B) Mixture of crystals and mother liquor
quiz.explanation: Massecuite is the mixture of sugar crystals and molasses that comes from the pan.

quiz.q: In a batch centrifugal, what is the purpose of washing?
quiz.explanation: Washing with water or steam removes the molasses film from crystal surfaces.

quiz.q: What is a typical screen opening size for a batch centrifugal?
quiz.explanation: Fine screens of 0.06Ã¢Â€Â“0.08 mm retain sugar crystals while letting molasses through.

quiz.q: What happens if the centrifugal screen is torn?
quiz.explanation: Torn screens allow crystals to pass through, causing sugar loss.

quiz.q: How much wash water is typically used in a batch centrifugal?
quiz.explanation: Using 3Ã¢Â€Â“5% water by weight of massecuite is a good balance between washing and yield.

quiz.q: What is affination?
options: A) Mixing raw sugar with heavy syrup to remove molasses film
B) Boiling sugar to high supersaturation
quiz.explanation: Affination softens and removes the molasses coating on raw sugar crystals.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of affination syrup?
quiz.explanation: Affination syrup (70Ã¢Â€Â“75 Brix) softens the molasses film so it can be washed off.

quiz.q: What temperature range is recommended for affination washing?
quiz.explanation: Water at 60Ã¢Â€Â“70Ã‚Â°C effectively removes molasses without dissolving too much sugar.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of affination?
options: B) Reduces color and ash in raw sugar
quiz.explanation: Affination reduces color, ash, and impurities by 50Ã¢Â€Â“70%, improving sugar quality.

quiz.q: What is final molasses?
options: A) Molasses from the first strike
B) Molasses left after maximum sugar extraction
quiz.explanation: Final molasses is the heavy syrup remaining after all recoverable sugar is crystallized.

quiz.q: What is a common use of molasses in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Molasses is widely used as an energy-rich animal feed mixed with roughage.

quiz.q: How much ethanol can be produced from one tonne of molasses?
quiz.explanation: Fermentation of one tonne of molasses yields about 250Ã¢Â€Â“300 liters of ethanol.

quiz.q: What is a key parameter to control during molasses exhaustion?
quiz.explanation: Controlling supersaturation and temperature ensures maximum sugar crystallization from molasses.

quiz.q: What is crystal size distribution (CSD)?
options: A) The average size of crystals
B) The range of crystal sizes in a sample
quiz.explanation: CSD describes the spread of crystal sizes, indicating uniformity.

quiz.q: Why is uniform crystal size important?
options: B) It improves centrifugation and washing
quiz.explanation: Uniform crystals centrifuge and wash more efficiently, leading to better quality and yield.

quiz.q: How is CSD measured in a lab?
options: B) Using a set of sieves
quiz.explanation: Sieving separates crystals by size, and the fractions are weighed to determine distribution.

quiz.q: What is a typical moisture content for white sugar?
quiz.explanation: White sugar should have very low moisture, typically below 0.05%, to prevent caking.

quiz.q: What does ICUMSA measure?
quiz.explanation: ICUMSA units measure color; lower values indicate whiter sugar.

quiz.q: What is a simple field method to check crystal size?
options: A) Use a magnifier and ruler
quiz.explanation: A magnifier and ruler allow approximate measurement of crystal dimensions.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see many fine crystals in your sugar?
options: B) Reduce supersaturation or add more seed
quiz.explanation: Reducing supersaturation or adding seed helps control nucleation and reduce fines.
